newsitem.title: USA: Mass. gets emergency aid from feds, Maine, NH wait.
newsitem.headline: Mass. gets emergency aid from feds, Maine, NH wait.

text.p: Five counties in eastern Massachusetts which were hit by a fierce weekend rainstorm were granted federal emergency aid, but Maine and New Hampshire are still awaiting Washington's assessment.
"I cannot tell you when we are going to get an answer on Maine and New Hampshire but it will be soon," said Janice Melton, a spokeswoman for the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Boston.
The emergency aid pays for temporary needs, like housing, debris removal and various public services.

The three New England states also asked President Clinton to issue a major disaster declaration, which would qualify them for additional aid, including help in rebuilding infrastructure, from roads to schools, as well as grants and low-interest loans for individuals for homes and businesses.

President Clinton may decide as soon as next week whether to issue a major disaster declaration, said the federal emergency official. She noted that Maine and New Hampshire might not qualify for the temporary emergency aid, but instead obtain the bigger relief package.

Teams in each of the three states are out surveying the damage caused by floods and fallen trees, while residents in a few seaside communities, like Lawrence, Mass., about 45 miles north of Boston, are still bailing out.

Some of the states' problems are interelated. For instance, flooding along the Merrimack River, one of New Hampshire's main rivers, is one of the reasons a 15-block section of Lawrence is under four to six feet of water, Massachusetts officials said.
David Rodham, the state's assistant secretary of public safety, said that the Merrimack was expected to crest by early today and should be starting to recede.

Two residential communities that straddle Boston also were particulary hard hit, as at least 1,000 homes in Quincy, eight miles south of Boston, suffered major damage. Homes in Revere, three miles north of Boston, were hit just as hard.

"They both just had a tremendous amount of flooding in the city and low spots, not necessarily due to the ocean, just due to the rain," said Rodham, explaining the floods rose as high as cars' headlights as they washed through basements.

New Hampshire is having its own problems with water, as it might take as long as six weeks to fully restore water supplies to some residents of Rockingham County, which is on the state's short stretch of seashore, a state official said.
The Red Cross is assisting, and the New Hampshire National Guard is supplying water trucks, said Gregg Champlin, spokesman for the state Office of Emergency Management.
Champlin said he hoped the surveys would be done by Friday afternoon, but declined to release any preliminary estimates.

So far, Maine has said it expects that at least $10 million of damage was done by the powerful nor'easter, while Boston has estimated damagee at $11 million. Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which runs Boston's subways, sees $15 million of damage in the wake of the storm.
In Maine, where Gov. Angus King is seeking federal aid for the state's two southernmost counties, York and Cumberland, Portand residents had to boil their water until noon Thursday.

While water pressure was restored yesterday after repair crews fixed a supply pipeline, the water still had to be boiled until tests were completed, explained Lynette Miller, as spokeswoman for Maine's Emergency Management Agency.
She added that secondary roads and highways, including the stretch of the Maine Turnpike in Portland, were severely damaged by washouts.

"We are looking at the usual panoply of roads, bridges and culverts (that need repairs), she said. For example, in Westbrook, a few miles west of Portland, two bridges were severely damaged along with one dam, while two dams were hit in Scarborough, just south of Portland.
